decks.name: Ports & protocols
decks.blurb: Port-number recall is the cheapest set of points on the exam. Know the secure/insecure pairs cold.
cards: FTP — data (20) and control (21). Cleartext; replace with SFTP (22) or FTPS (990).
SSH, SCP, SFTP — encrypted remote admin and file transfer. The secure replacement for Telnet and FTP.
Telnet — cleartext remote administration. Credentials visible on the wire; disable it.
SMTP — mail transfer between servers. Cleartext by default; 587 is the submission port.
TACACS+ — Cisco AAA. Encrypts the entire payload and separates authentication from authorization (RADIUS does not).
DNS — name resolution, UDP for queries and TCP for zone transfers. A common exfiltration and C2 channel.
DHCP — server (67) and client (68). Rogue DHCP servers enable on-path attacks.
TFTP — trivial file transfer, UDP, no authentication. Often used for network device configs.
HTTP — unencrypted web. Should redirect to 443 with HSTS.
Kerberos — Windows domain authentication. Ticket-based; targeted by golden and silver ticket attacks.
POP3 — mail retrieval, downloads and removes. Secure version is 995.
NTP — time synchronization. Critical for log correlation and Kerberos; also abused for amplification.
RPC and NetBIOS — legacy Windows services. Should never be exposed to the internet.
IMAP — mail retrieval, leaves mail on the server. Secure version is 993.
SNMP — agent queries (161) and traps (162). Use v3 for authentication and encryption.
LDAP — directory queries, cleartext. Secure version is 636.
HTTPS — HTTP over TLS. The baseline for all web traffic.
SMB — Windows file sharing. The vector for EternalBlue and most ransomware lateral movement.
SMTPS (465) and SMTP submission with STARTTLS (587) — encrypted mail sending from clients.
Syslog — log forwarding, UDP and cleartext. Use 6514 for syslog over TLS.
LDAPS — LDAP over TLS. The secure directory query port.
IMAPS — IMAP over TLS.
POP3S — POP3 over TLS.
Microsoft SQL Server — database. Never expose directly to the internet.
Oracle database listener.
RADIUS — authentication (1812) and accounting (1813). Encrypts only the password, not the whole payload.
MySQL / MariaDB database.
RDP — Windows remote desktop. The single most attacked port for ransomware entry; put it behind a VPN or gateway.
SIP — VoIP signalling, cleartext (5060) and TLS (5061).
Syslog over TLS — the encrypted log-forwarding port.
FTPS — FTP over TLS control channel.
Alternate HTTP and HTTPS — common for proxies, management consoles, and app servers.

decks.name: Acronyms
decks.blurb: SY0-701 stems use bare acronyms and expect you to know them without expansion.
cards: AAA
Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting — who you are, what you may do, and what you did.
ACL
Access Control List — ordered permit/deny rules on a firewall, router, or file system.
AES
Advanced Encryption Standard — the symmetric block cipher standard (128/192/256-bit keys).
ALE
Annualized Loss Expectancy — SLE × ARO. The yearly expected cost of a risk.
APT
Advanced Persistent Threat — a well-resourced actor, usually nation-state, focused on long-term stealthy access.
ARO
Annualized Rate of Occurrence — how many times per year a loss event is expected.
ASLR
Address Space Layout Randomization — randomizes memory layout to frustrate buffer-overflow exploits.
BIA
Business Impact Analysis — identifies critical processes and sets RTO and RPO.
BPA
Business Partnership Agreement — defines responsibilities between two partnering businesses.
CA
Certificate Authority — issues and signs digital certificates; the root of PKI trust.
CASB
Cloud Access Security Broker — enforces policy between users and cloud services.
CRL
Certificate Revocation List — the published list of revoked certificates. OCSP is the real-time alternative.
CVE
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — the unique identifier for a specific known flaw.
CVSS
Common Vulnerability Scoring System — the 0–10 severity score for a vulnerability.
DLP
Data Loss Prevention — inspects and blocks sensitive data leaving via mail, web, or endpoints.
DMARC
Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance — tells receivers what to do when SPF/DKIM fail.
DKIM
DomainKeys Identified Mail — cryptographically signs outbound mail headers.
EDR
Endpoint Detection and Response — behavioural endpoint monitoring with investigation and rollback.
FIM
File Integrity Monitoring — alerts when protected files change unexpectedly.
HSM
Hardware Security Module — tamper-resistant appliance that generates and stores keys; keys never leave it.
IaC
Infrastructure as Code — configuration defined in version-controlled templates, deployed by pipeline.
IdP
Identity Provider — authenticates the user and issues assertions in a federated login.
IoC
Indicator of Compromise — an artifact showing a breach occurred (hash, domain, IP, registry key).
MDM
Mobile Device Management — enrolls, configures, and remotely wipes mobile endpoints.
MFA
Multifactor Authentication — two or more of: something you know, have, or are.
MOU / MOA
Memorandum of Understanding / Agreement — a non-binding statement of intent between parties.
MSA
Master Service Agreement — the umbrella contract; individual work is scoped in SOWs beneath it.
MTBF
Mean Time Between Failures — average uptime between failures of a repairable system.
MTTR
Mean Time To Repair — average time to restore service after a failure.
NAC
Network Access Control — checks device posture before granting network access.
OCSP
Online Certificate Status Protocol — real-time revocation checking; stapling moves the check to the server.
PKI
Public Key Infrastructure — the CAs, certificates, and policies that bind keys to identities.
RPO
Recovery Point Objective — the maximum tolerable amount of data loss, measured in time.
RTO
Recovery Time Objective — the maximum tolerable time to restore a service.
SAML
Security Assertion Markup Language — XML-based federation, common for enterprise web SSO.
SASE
Secure Access Service Edge — cloud-delivered networking and security (SD-WAN plus SWG, CASB, ZTNA).
SCAP
Security Content Automation Protocol — standard formats for automated compliance and vulnerability checks.
SIEM
Security Information and Event Management — central log aggregation, correlation, and alerting.
SLA
Service Level Agreement — the committed performance and availability levels, with penalties.
SLE
Single Loss Expectancy — asset value × exposure factor. The cost of one occurrence.
SOAR
Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response — playbook-driven automation of SOC workflows.
SOW
Statement of Work — the specific deliverables, timeline, and pricing under an MSA.
SPF
Sender Policy Framework — DNS record listing which hosts may send mail for a domain.
SSO
Single Sign-On — one authentication grants access to multiple applications.
TPM
Trusted Platform Module — on-board chip storing keys and measurements; enables full-disk encryption and secure boot.
UEBA
User and Entity Behavior Analytics — baselines normal behaviour and flags deviations.
XDR
Extended Detection and Response — correlates detection across endpoint, network, identity, and cloud.
ZTNA
Zero Trust Network Access — per-session, identity-and-posture-based access to a specific application.

decks.name: Crypto quick recall
decks.blurb: Which algorithm does what, and which are dead. Exam items hinge on picking the right category.
cards: AES
Symmetric block cipher. Confidentiality. 128/192/256-bit keys. The default choice for data at rest.
RSA
Asymmetric. Key exchange, encryption, and digital signatures. Needs large keys (2048-bit minimum).
ECC / ECDSA
Asymmetric using elliptic curves. Same strength as RSA at much smaller key sizes — ideal for mobile and IoT.
Diffie-Hellman (DH / ECDHE)
Key exchange only — never encrypts data. Ephemeral versions (DHE/ECDHE) provide perfect forward secrecy.
SHA-256 / SHA-3
Hashing. Integrity only — one-way, no key, not encryption.
MD5 and SHA-1
Broken hashes. Collision-vulnerable; acceptable only for non-security checksums.
HMAC
Hash-based Message Authentication Code — hash plus a shared secret. Provides integrity AND authenticity.
bcrypt / scrypt / Argon2 / PBKDF2
Key derivation functions for password storage. Deliberately slow and salted to resist cracking.
Salt vs pepper
Salt: unique random value stored with each hash, defeats rainbow tables. Pepper: a secret value stored separately, not in the database.
Digital signature
Hash the message, encrypt the hash with the SENDER'S PRIVATE key. Gives integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation.
Encrypting for a recipient
Encrypt with the RECIPIENT'S PUBLIC key; only their private key can open it.
Perfect forward secrecy
A unique ephemeral session key per session, so a stolen long-term private key cannot decrypt past traffic.
TLS 1.3
Current standard. Removed RSA key exchange, static DH, and legacy ciphers; mandates forward secrecy.
Tokenization vs encryption
Tokenization swaps data for a meaningless reference held in a vault; encryption is mathematically reversible with a key.
Data masking
Irreversibly obscures data for display or test use (showing only the last four digits).
Blockchain / open public ledger
Distributed append-only record; integrity through chained hashes and consensus, not confidentiality.
Key escrow
A third party holds a copy of keys for lawful recovery — a recovery control and an insider risk.
Steganography
Hiding data inside other data (an image or audio file). Concealment, not encryption.

decks.name: Frameworks, laws & roles
decks.blurb: Domain 5 is 20% of the exam and is mostly definitional — the cheapest domain to lock in.
cards: GDPR
EU privacy regulation. Applies to EU residents' data wherever processed. Rights include access, rectification, and erasure; 72-hour breach notification.
PCI DSS
Payment card industry standard. Contractual, not a law. Governs storage and handling of cardholder data.
HIPAA
US healthcare law protecting PHI. Covers providers, plans, and their business associates.
SOX
Sarbanes-Oxley — US financial reporting integrity for public companies. Drives change control and separation of duties.
International standard for an Information Security Management System (ISMS). Certifiable.
NIST CSF
Voluntary framework: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
800-53: control catalog for federal systems. 800-171: protecting controlled unclassified information in non-federal systems.
SOC 2 Type I vs Type II
Type I: control design at a point in time. Type II: operating effectiveness over a period (usually 6–12 months).
Data owner
Senior business role accountable for classification and access decisions for a data set.
Data custodian / steward
Implements and maintains the controls the owner specifies — the hands-on technical role.
Data controller vs processor
Controller decides why and how data is processed; processor acts on the controller's instructions.
DPO
Data Protection Officer — required under GDPR for certain organizations; oversees privacy compliance independently.
Due diligence vs due care
Due diligence is investigating and researching. Due care is acting on what you found.
Risk appetite vs risk tolerance
Appetite: how much risk the organization is willing to pursue. Tolerance: acceptable variation around a specific risk.
Four risk responses
Accept, Avoid, Mitigate (reduce), Transfer (share, e.g. insurance).
Residual vs inherent risk
Inherent: risk before controls. Residual: what remains after controls. Only the owner may formally accept residual risk.
KRI vs KPI
KRI is a leading indicator warning that risk is rising. KPI measures performance against a goal.
RACI
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — assigns ownership for tasks and decisions.
Control types
Preventive, Detective, Corrective, Deterrent, Compensating, Directive.
Control categories
Technical, Managerial, Operational, Physical.
Right to be forgotten
The data subject's right to erasure. Requires a data inventory to locate every copy.
Attestation
A formal signed statement that controls are in place — the output of an audit or assessment.

decks.name: Sequences & numbers
decks.blurb: Ordered lists and threshold numbers the exam expects verbatim.
cards: Incident response phases
Preparation → Detection → Analysis → Containment → Eradication → Recovery → Lessons Learned.
Order of volatility
CPU registers/cache → RAM → network state and running processes → disk → remote logs → archival media.
Digital forensics sequence
Legal hold → acquisition (bit-for-bit image) → hash to prove integrity → analysis on the copy → reporting. Chain of custody throughout.
Change management sequence
Request → impact analysis → CAB approval → test → scheduled implementation → validation → documentation. Backout plan defined before implementation.
Vulnerability management cycle
Identify → analyze and validate → prioritize → remediate or accept → rescan to verify → report.
3-2-1 backup rule
Three copies of the data, on two different media types, with one stored offsite.
RTO vs RPO
RTO looks forward: how long until service is back. RPO looks backward: how much data loss is acceptable.
Exam facts
SY0-701: maximum 90 questions in 90 minutes. Scored 100–900; 750 passes. 750 is NOT 75% correct — items are weighted and PBQs carry more.
Domain weighting
1 General Security Concepts 12% · 2 Threats/Vulnerabilities/Mitigations 22% · 3 Security Architecture 18% · 4 Security Operations 28% · 5 Program Management 20%.
Tabletop vs simulation vs failover
Tabletop: discussion only. Simulation: a realistic exercise without touching production. Failover/parallel: actually cut over to the recovery site.
Penetration test knowledge levels
Known environment (white box): full information. Partially known (gray box): limited. Unknown (black box): none.
Agreement hierarchy
MSA is the umbrella contract; SOW scopes specific work; SLA sets performance levels; NDA covers confidentiality; MOU/MOA state non-binding intent.
Zero Trust planes
Control plane: adaptive identity, policy engine, policy administrator. Data plane: policy enforcement point acting on each request.
CIA vs AAA vs non-repudiation
CIA: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. AAA: Authentication, Authorization, Accounting. Non-repudiation: proof the actor cannot deny the action — from digital signatures and logging.
